title: A Door of Hope
subtitle: Hosea, Joel, Amos & Obadiah in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin:
These four prophets speak to a people who had drifted. Hosea keeps a door open for a wife who left, and hears God say, How can I give you up? Joel walks a field stripped bare by locusts and hears a promise to restore the years they ate. Amos, a herdsman from the hills, holds a plumb line beside a leaning wall and calls for justice to roll on like rivers. Obadiah looks up at a nest built among the stars and tells the proud they will come down.

This book walks through them in forty short poems, in five parts: two for Hosea, then Joel, Amos and Obadiah. Each poem sits beside a picture and under a single line of Scripture. The pictures stay with the things the prophets saw—a door in a valley of trouble, a lily heavy with dew, a stripped fig tree, a stick pulled from the fire, a mended tent—and leave the faces to your imagination.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it. Open the books of Hosea, Joel, Amos and Obadiah alongside this book, and let the real words have the last word.

paintings.title: a living parable
paintings.epigraph: “Y ahweh’s word that came to Hosea the son of Beeri”
paintings.poem:
some prophets
were handed a scroll.

Hosea
was handed a life.

his own house
became the sermon:
a promise made,
a promise broken,
a door he kept
not locking.

the nation would watch him
and, if they had eyes,
see themselves.

and see, standing in the doorway,
the kind of love
that God had been
all along.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Let your eyes rest on the brushwork and light around the open threshold: what quiet prayer rises in you when you read, “and see, standing in the doorway, the kind of love that God had been all along”?

paintings.title: new names
paintings.epigraph: “they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’”
paintings.poem:
the children's names
were hard to say out loud.

no mercy.
not my people.

names like
a door shutting.

but the same breath
opened it again:

in the very place
where they were called
not mine,

they will be called
children
of the living God.

God does not leave
the last word
at no.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Linger with the movement in “new names” (Hosea 1:9–10) from “the children's names were hard to say out loud” to “God does not leave the last word at no”—where do you find yourself along that arc today?

paintings.title: who gave the grain
paintings.epigraph: “she didn’t know that I gave her the grain, the new wine, and the oil”
paintings.poem:
she thanked the wrong hands.

the bread came
from somewhere,
so she guessed.

the wine came
from somewhere,
so she guessed again.

all along
the one who filled her table
was standing
just outside the light,

giving,
and giving,
and not being named.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Notice how “who gave the grain” (Hosea 2:8) arrives at: “all along the one who filled her table was standing just outside the light, giving, and giving, and not being named.” Who in your life is walking a hard stretch of road today and needs you to share this grace with them?

paintings.title: thorns on the road
paintings.epigraph: “I will hedge up your way with thorns”
paintings.poem:
sometimes the road
closes.

the thing you ran toward
won't let you catch it.

the door you knocked on
stays shut.

it feels like
being lost.

it may be
being kept.

she said,
I will go home.
it was better there.

the thorns
were a hedge
around the way back.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What if the most important thing you remember before tonight is the quiet lesson of Hosea 2:6–7: “the thorns were a hedge around the way back”?

paintings.title: I will allure her
paintings.epigraph: “I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her.”
paintings.poem:
after all of it,
you would expect
a lecture.

instead:
a quiet place.
no crowds.
no voices competing.

and God
speaking tenderly.

the wilderness
is not always punishment.

sometimes it is
the only place
quiet enough
to hear
that you are still wanted.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Imagine standing inside this frame beside the still, unhurried voice: what hurry or noise in your week begins to fade when you hear, “sometimes it is the only place quiet enough to hear that you are still wanted”?

paintings.title: a door of hope
paintings.epigraph: “she will respond there, as in the days of her youth”
paintings.poem:
Achor was
the valley of trouble,
a name
they would rather forget.

and God said,
that's where I'll put the door.

not around the trouble.
through it.

the place you cannot
talk about

becomes the place
you step out of
singing,

like you did
when you were young
and the whole road
was ahead of you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Read the closing words aloud in the stillness: “the place you cannot talk about becomes the place you step out of singing, like you did when you were young and the whole road was ahead of you.” What part of your heart feels most searched or comforted by Hosea 2:15 right now?

paintings.title: betrothed
paintings.epigraph: “I will betroth you to me forever.”
paintings.poem:
not a contract.
a betrothal.

and the gifts
he brings to it:

righteousness,
justice,
loving kindness,
compassion,
faithfulness.

nothing here
is on loan.

forever
is the word
he chose.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Hosea 2:19–20, grace meets us right beside the quiet centerpiece of “betrothed”: how does the closing thought—“forever is the word he chose”—steady your footing for the road ahead?

paintings.title: go again
paintings.epigraph: “even as Y ahweh loves the children of Israel”
paintings.poem:
go again,
God said.
not once. again.

so he paid
silver and barley
and brought her home.

stay with me,
he told her.
I will be yours too.

this is how
Yahweh loves:

he goes again.
he pays again.
he brings us home.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If today’s painting of “go again” (Hosea 3:1–2) hung beside the door you walk out of this morning, how would its final line—“he pays again. he brings us home”—shape your choices?

paintings.title: the land mourns
paintings.epigraph: “Therefore the land will mourn”
paintings.poem:
no truth.
no goodness.
no knowing God.

and the fields
feel it first.

the ground goes quiet.
the birds thin out.
even the streams
grow shy.

we think our choices
stay inside us.

they don't.

the whole land
leans in
to hear
whether we'll turn.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Every stop on the Pilgrim Walk shows how God meets us in ordinary places (Hosea 4:1–3)—where in your own home or work today does “the whole land leans in to hear whether we'll turn” ring true?

paintings.title: as sure as sunrise
paintings.epigraph: “As surely as the sun rises, Y ahweh will appear. He will come to us like the rain, like the spring rain that waters the earth.”
paintings.poem:
come,
let's go back.

the one who wounded
is the one who binds.

press on to know him.
not once.
keep pressing.

you don't have to
talk the sun
into rising.

you don't have to
earn the spring rain.

he will come.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Take a slow breath and read the final line again: “you don't have to earn the spring rain. he will come.” How would you walk through the next hour differently if you carried that truth with you?

paintings.title: morning cloud
paintings.epigraph: “For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice”
paintings.poem:
your love,
he said,
is a morning cloud.

there at dawn.
gone by midmorning.

and still
he didn't ask for more
smoke on the altar.

he asked for
mercy.

for knowing him.

a love that stays
past the heat of the day.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Think of a season when you knew the feeling of “your love, he said, is a morning cloud.” Looking through the lens of Hosea 6:4–6, what does it mean to discover that “a love that stays past the heat of the day”?

paintings.title: half-baked
paintings.epigraph: “Ephraim is a pancake not turned over.”
paintings.poem:
burnt on one side.
raw on the other.

nobody turned it.

and gray hairs
here and there,
and he doesn't
realize it.

a life can slip away
while we are busy
leaning toward
everyone else.

turn
while it's still
warm.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look closely at the quiet centerpiece of “half-baked” in this painting (Hosea 7:8–9)—if you could leave one anxious weight beside it today, what would you set down?

paintings.title: fallow ground
paintings.epigraph: “Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Y ahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you.”
paintings.poem:
the field
has been resting
too long.

hard on top.
nothing gets in.

so break it.
not all at once,
one furrow.

sow righteousness.
reap kindness.

and then
wait for the rain
you can't make,

which he has promised
to send.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Let your eyes rest on the brushwork and light around the quiet centerpiece of “fallow ground”: what quiet prayer rises in you when you read, “and then wait for the rain you can't make, which he has promised to send”?

paintings.title: learning to walk
paintings.epigraph: “Yet I taught Ephraim to walk. I took them by his arms”
paintings.poem:
when Israel was a child
I loved him.

I called my son
out of Egypt.

I held his arms
while he wobbled.

I bent down
and fed him.

cords of love,
he says.
not chains.

the kind of rope
a parent holds
so a child
can fall
and not be lost.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Linger with the movement in “learning to walk” (Hosea 11:1–4) from “when Israel was a child I loved him” to “the kind of rope a parent holds so a child can fall and not be lost”—where do you find yourself along that arc today?

paintings.title: how can I give you up
paintings.epigraph: “How can I give you up, Ephraim? How can I hand you over, Israel?”
paintings.poem:
everything had been said.
every warning given.

and then
this.

how can I?

God does not
turn cold.

my heart is turned
within me,
he says.

I am God,
not a man.

which means
the mercy
goes deeper
than the anger
ever could.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Notice how “how can I give you up” (Hosea 11:8–9) arrives at: “which means the mercy goes deeper than the anger ever could.” Who in your life is walking a hard stretch of road today and needs you to share this grace with them?

paintings.title: like the dew
paintings.epigraph: “I will be like the dew to Israel. He will blossom like the lily”
paintings.poem:
to the ones
who come back,
God says:

I will heal.
I will love freely.

I will be the dew,
quiet,
every morning.

you will bloom.
you will root deep.
people will sit
in your shade.

your fruit
comes from me.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What if the most important thing you remember before tonight is the quiet lesson of Hosea 14:4–7: “you will root deep. your fruit comes from me”?

paintings.title: tell your children
paintings.epigraph: “T ell your children about it, and have your children tell their children”
paintings.poem:
first one swarm.
then what it left,
another took.

then what that one left,
another.

by the end
there was nothing
but stubble.

and the prophet said:
tell your children.

not so they'd be afraid.

so they'd know
what happened,
and who they ran to
when it did.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Imagine standing inside this frame beside the quiet centerpiece of “tell your children”: what hurry or noise in your week begins to fade when you hear, “so they'd know what happened, and who they ran to when it did”?

paintings.title: joy has withered
paintings.epigraph: “for joy has withered away from the sons of men.”
paintings.poem:
the vine.
the fig.
the pomegranate.
the palm.

all of them,
dry.

and something else
withered with them.

it's hard to sing
over an empty barn.

grief is allowed here.

the Bible
leaves room
to say so.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Read the closing words aloud in the stillness: “the Bible leaves room to say so.” What part of your heart feels most searched or comforted by Joel 1:10–12 right now?

paintings.title: even the animals
paintings.epigraph: “Yes, the animals of the field pant to you”
paintings.poem:
the brooks
have dried up.

the animals
stand at the empty bed
and lift their heads.

the prophet
takes it as a prayer.

if even the animals
turn their faces
toward you,

Lord,
so will I.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Joel 1:19–20, grace meets us right beside the quiet brook: how does the closing thought—“if even the animals turn their faces toward you, Lord, so will I”—steady your footing for the road ahead?

paintings.title: tear your heart
paintings.epigraph: “Tear your heart, and not your garments, and turn to Yahweh, your God”
paintings.poem:
yet even now,
he says.

after the swarm.
after the dark.

even now.

the robe can be torn
without anything
changing.

so tear the heart.

open it
to the one who is

gracious,
merciful,
slow to anger,

full
of loving kindness.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If today’s painting of “tear your heart” (Joel 2:12–13) hung beside the door you walk out of this morning, how would its final line—“open it to the one who is gracious, merciful, slow to anger, full of loving kindness”—shape your choices?

paintings.title: who knows?
paintings.epigraph: “Who knows? He may turn and relent, and leave a blessing behind him”
paintings.poem:
who knows?

that's all the prophet
could promise.

not a guarantee.
a direction.

turn,
and see what
he leaves behind.

a little grain.
a little wine.

enough
to begin
worshiping again.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Every stop on the Pilgrim Walk shows how God meets us in ordinary places (Joel 2:14)—where in your own home or work today does “enough to begin worshiping again” ring true?

paintings.title: early and latter rain
paintings.epigraph: “Land, don’t be afraid. Be glad and rejoice, for Y ahweh has done great things.”
paintings.poem:
he speaks to the land
first.

don't be afraid.

then to the animals.
don't be afraid.

then to his people:
be glad.

the pastures spring up.
the fig tree remembers
how to bear.

the early rain.
the latter rain.
as before.

the threshing floors
full.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Take a slow breath and read the final line again: “the threshing floors full.” How would you walk through the next hour differently if you carried that truth with you?

paintings.title: the years the locust ate
paintings.epigraph: “You will have plenty to eat, and be satisfied, and will praise the name of Yahweh, your God, who has dealt wondrously with you”
paintings.poem:
he doesn't just
give back the field.

he gives back
the years.

the ones that went
to the swarm.

the ones you thought
were only loss.

nobody else
can pay you back
in time.

he says
he will.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Think of a season when you knew the feeling of “he doesn't just give back the field.” Looking through the lens of Joel 2:25–26, what does it mean to discover that “nobody else can pay you back in time. he says he will”?

paintings.title: on all flesh
paintings.epigraph: “I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh”
paintings.poem:
sons and daughters.
old men and young men.

servants too.
the handmaids too.

no one too young.
no one too old.
no one too low.

he didn't pour it
on a chosen few
this time.

all flesh.

which means
your kitchen,
your street,
your ordinary name.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look closely at the name by which He calls you in this painting (Joel 2:28–29)—if you could leave one anxious weight beside it today, what would you set down?

paintings.title: a fountain from the house
paintings.epigraph: “a fountain will flow out from Yahweh’s house”
paintings.poem:
the heavens shake,
and still
he is a refuge.

the earth trembles,
and still
a stronghold.

and after it all,
a fountain
from his house,

running down
into the dry valley,

watering
the places
nothing grew.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Let your eyes rest on the brushwork and light around the low road through the valley: what quiet prayer rises in you when you read, “and after it all, a fountain from his house, running down into the dry valley, watering the places nothing grew”?

paintings.title: for three, and for four
paintings.epigraph: “because they have sold the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals”
paintings.poem:
Damascus. Gaza.
Tyre. Edom.

the crowd agreed
with every word.

Ammon. Moab.
Judah.

yes, preacher. them.

then the circle closed:
Israel.

a person, sold
for the price
of a pair of sandals.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Linger with the movement in “for three, and for four” (Amos 2:6) from “Damascus. Gaza” to “a person, sold for the price of a pair of sandals”—where do you find yourself along that arc today?

paintings.title: two walking
paintings.epigraph: “Do two walk together, unless they have agreed?”
paintings.poem:
two walk together
because they've agreed
where they're going.

you can't walk
with God

and head somewhere
he isn't.

the good news
is that he's still
on the road,

waiting
for you
to fall back
into step.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Notice how “two walking” (Amos 3:3) arrives at: “the good news is that he's still on the road, waiting for you to fall back into step.” Who in your life is walking a hard stretch of road today and needs you to share this grace with them?

paintings.title: a stick from the fire
paintings.epigraph: “you were like a burning stick plucked out of the fire; yet you haven’t returned to me”
paintings.poem:
hunger.
drought.
blight.

five times
the same refrain:
you haven't returned to me.

and in the middle of it,
this:

you were a stick
pulled out of the fire.

still smoking.
still here.

rescued
is not the end
of the story.

returning is.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What if the most important thing you remember before tonight is the quiet lesson of Amos 4:11: “rescued is not the end of the story. returning is”?

paintings.title: seek him and live
paintings.epigraph: “seek him who made the Pleiades and Orion, and turns the shadow of death into the morning”
paintings.poem:
a herdsman
knows the night sky.

he knows which stars
come before the dawn.

and he says:
don't seek the shrines.

seek the one
who hung those stars,

who turns
the shadow of death
into morning.

seek him,
and live.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Imagine standing inside this frame beside the quiet stars overhead: what hurry or noise in your week begins to fade when you hear, “seek the one who hung those stars, who turns the shadow of death into morning. seek him, and live”?

paintings.title: the noise of your songs
paintings.epigraph: “Take away from me the noise of your songs! I will not listen to the music of your harps.”
paintings.poem:
the songs
were beautiful.

the harps
in tune.

and God said,
take it away.

because down the hill
a poor man
was losing his coat.

worship
was never meant
to drown out
the cry at the gate.

let justice
roll on like rivers.

then sing.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Read the closing words aloud in the stillness: “let justice roll on like rivers. then sing.” What part of your heart feels most searched or comforted by Amos 5:21–24 right now?

paintings.title: beds of ivory
paintings.epigraph: “but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph.”
paintings.poem:
soft cushions.
the best lamb.
wine by the bowl.
new songs every night.

none of it
was the problem.

the problem
was one line:

they were not grieved.

a whole people
breaking
just outside,

and nobody
at the feast
could feel it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Amos 6:4–6, grace meets us right beside the quiet centerpiece of “beds of ivory”: how does the closing thought—“a whole people breaking just outside, and nobody at the feast could feel it”—steady your footing for the road ahead?

paintings.title: he is small
paintings.epigraph: “How could Jacob stand? For he is small.”
paintings.poem:
twice the prophet
saw what was coming.

twice
he stopped it
with a prayer.

not
they deserve better.

just:
forgive.
he is small.

and twice
God relented.

never underestimate
the one who stands
in the gap
and pleads.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If today’s painting of “he is small” (Amos 7:2–3) hung beside the door you walk out of this morning, how would its final line—“never underestimate the one who stands in the gap and pleads”—shape your choices?

paintings.title: the plumb line
paintings.epigraph: “Behold, I will set a plumb line in the middle of my people Israel.”
paintings.poem:
a string.
a weight.
nothing fancy.

hold it up
beside a wall

and the truth
is simply there.

no argument.
no shouting.

just straight
next to crooked.

God doesn't need
to exaggerate.

he only needs
to hold it still.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Every stop on the Pilgrim Walk shows how God meets us in ordinary places (Amos 7:7–8)—where in your own home or work today does “he only needs to hold it still” ring true?

paintings.title: a farmer of sycamore figs
paintings.epigraph: “I was a herdsman, and a farmer of sycamore figs”
paintings.poem:
they told him
to go home.

this is the king's
sanctuary.

and he said,
I'm not a prophet.

I tended flocks.
I worked fig trees.

Yahweh took me
from behind the sheep.

no pedigree.
no title.

just a man
who was told
go,

and went.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Take a slow breath and read the final line again: “just a man who was told go, and went.” How would you walk through the next hour differently if you carried that truth with you?

paintings.title: the fallen tent
paintings.epigraph: “In that day I will raise up the tent of David who is fallen”
paintings.poem:
after all the warnings,
the book turns
on one small word:

in that day.

the house has fallen.
the tent is torn.

and God says,
I will raise it.
I will close the gaps.
I will build it
as in the days of old.

he doesn't
throw away
what broke.

he mends it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Think of a season when you knew the feeling of “after all the warnings, the book turns on one small word: in that day.” Looking through the lens of Amos 9:11, what does it mean to discover that “he doesn't throw away what broke. he mends it”?

paintings.title: the plowman and the reaper
paintings.epigraph: “the plowman shall overtake the reaper”
paintings.poem:
the harvest
so heavy
it isn't finished

before the plowing
starts again.

the hills
running with sweet wine.

cities rebuilt.
gardens planted.

and the last line
is a promise:

I will plant them,
and they will no more
be plucked up.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look closely at the quiet centerpiece of “the plowman and the reaper” in this painting (Amos 9:13–15)—if you could leave one anxious weight beside it today, what would you set down?

paintings.title: the clefts of the rock
paintings.epigraph: “The pride of your heart has deceived you”
paintings.poem:
high in the rock,
Edom felt safe.

who could reach us
up here?

pride is like that.

it builds
on the highest ledge
and calls the view
wisdom.

but the one
who made the stars

can reach
any nest
set among them.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Let your eyes rest on the brushwork and light around the quiet stars overhead: what quiet prayer rises in you when you read, “but the one who made the stars can reach any nest set among them”?

paintings.title: on the other side
paintings.epigraph: “In the day that you stood on the other side”
paintings.poem:
strangers came
through Jacob's gates.

and Edom,
his own brother,
stood on the other side

and watched,
and then
joined in.

it rarely starts
with the blow.

it starts
with where
we choose
to stand.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Linger with the movement in “on the other side” (Obadiah 1:11) from “strangers came through Jacob's gates” to “it starts with where we choose to stand”—where do you find yourself along that arc today?

paintings.title: as you have done
paintings.epigraph: “As you have done, it will be done to you.”
paintings.poem:
don't gloat.
don't laugh
at the gate.
don't take
what they dropped.

don't stand at the crossroads
to cut off
the ones who ran.

the prophet
lists it all

so we'll know:

what we do
to the one who is falling

comes home to us.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Notice how “as you have done” (Obadiah 1:12–15) arrives at: “the prophet lists it all so we'll know: what we do to the one who is falling comes home to us.” Who in your life is walking a hard stretch of road today and needs you to share this grace with them?

paintings.title: the kingdom
paintings.epigraph: “the kingdom will be Yahweh’s.”
paintings.poem:
Edom's cliffs.
Israel's ruins.
nations rising.
nations falling.

and the shortest book
in the Old Testament

ends
in five words.

the kingdom
will be Yahweh's.

not Edom's.
not ours.

his.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What if the most important thing you remember before tonight is the quiet lesson of Obadiah 1:17–21: “not Edom's. not ours. his”?
